title: U-Net: Encoder–Decoder for Segmentation
hook: A U-shaped net that shrinks an image down to capture context, then rebuilds it pixel by pixel — with shortcuts that preserve fine detail. Now the workhorse inside diffusion models.
key_points: Symmetric encoder–decoder: the encoder compresses to capture context, the decoder upsamples back to full resolution.
Skip connections copy fine-grained features from encoder to decoder to keep sharp detail.
Designed for biomedical image segmentation, where labeled data is scarce.
Trains well from few annotated images using heavy data augmentation.
Later became the standard denoiser backbone inside diffusion models.
content_html: Ronneberger, Fischer, and Brox designed U-Net for biomedical image segmentation — labeling every pixel of an image — and showed it could train well from only a handful of annotated examples. Its U-shaped encoder–decoder with skip connections became a template far beyond medicine.
extra_html:
How it works

The encoder half progressively downsamples the image, capturing what is in it and where, in a compact representation. The decoder half upsamples back to full resolution to produce a per-pixel prediction. The key trick is skip connections: feature maps from each encoder stage are copied across to the matching decoder stage, so the output keeps the crisp spatial detail that downsampling would otherwise blur away.

Why it matters

U-Net made dense, pixel-level prediction practical even with small datasets, and it remains a go-to for segmentation. Its second life is arguably bigger: the architecture became the default network that diffusion models use to predict and remove noise, so today's image generators run on a descendant of this design.

related.title: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet)
related.hook: Stacking more layers used to make networks worse, not better. ResNet's fix — let each layer learn a tweak to its input — unlocked nets over 100 layers deep.

related.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
related.hook: Wreck an image into pure static one tiny step at a time, then train a network to undo it. Run the undo from random noise and you get a brand-new image.
